title: Why Is Qifu Technology (QFIN) Stock Down -18.47% Today?

# Key Takeaways

* **Sharply lower:** Qifu Technology ([QFIN](https://tickeron.com/ticker/QFIN/)) shares fell about 18.47% to roughly $9.40 from a prior close of $11.53.
* **Earnings-driven move:** Disappointing second-quarter results and weak third-quarter guidance triggered the selloff.
* **Revenue miss:** Total net revenue fell 31.6% year over year, while non-GAAP earnings per ADS came in well below consensus.
* **Analyst downgrades:** Morgan Stanley, Citigroup and JPMorgan cut ratings and price targets, compounding the pressure.
* **Regulatory and sector headwinds:** Tightening oversight and industry-wide liquidity stress in China's consumer-credit market remain key overhangs.
* **What to watch:** Traders are focused on asset-quality trends, loan volume stabilization and further analyst revisions.

# Opening Summary

Qifu Technology ([QFIN](https://tickeron.com/ticker/QFIN/)), a leading China-based, AI-empowered credit technology platform that connects individual borrowers with financial institutions, is down sharply in Wednesday's trading. The stock fell roughly 18.47% to about $9.40, down from a prior session close of $11.53, pushing shares toward the lower end of their 52-week range. The selloff was triggered by second-quarter results that missed expectations on revenue and earnings, a cautious outlook for the third quarter, and a wave of analyst downgrades citing weak loan volume and lingering regulatory risk.

# Earnings Results and Weak Guidance

The primary catalyst for the decline was Qifu Technology's second-quarter 2026 report. Total net revenue declined 31.6% year over year to RMB 3.57 billion (about $525.6 million), while non-GAAP earnings per American depositary share came in at RMB 3.72 ($0.55), well short of the RMB 7.57 consensus estimate. Net income dropped to roughly RMB 401 million from RMB 1.73 billion a year earlier, partly reflecting a one-time tax charge of about RMB 500 million tied to a revised interpretation of certain tax treatments.

Investors were also rattled by management's outlook. The company guided to third-quarter net income of RMB 360 million to RMB 460 million, implying a substantial year-over-year decline, and warned that risk metrics could deteriorate as industry stress continues. Total loan facilitation and origination volume fell 25.1% year over year to RMB 63.4 billion, reflecting a deliberate shift toward tighter underwriting and lower loan volumes.

# Analyst Downgrades

The weak results triggered a rapid repricing by sell-side analysts, deepening the selloff. Morgan Stanley downgraded [QFIN](https://tickeron.com/ticker/QFIN/) from Overweight to Equal Weight and cut its price target to $13 from $25, citing a one-off tax charge and regulatory headwinds that could pressure loan volume and credit quality. Citigroup issued a double downgrade to Sell from Buy, slashing its target to $8 from $30.10 and describing the quarter as "soft." JPMorgan moved the stock to Underweight with a $9 target, while Jefferies lowered its price objective to $15.40 from $20.40 even as it maintained a Buy rating. The flurry of cuts reinforced the bearish narrative around slowing growth and shrinking returns.

# Sector and Regulatory Pressure

Beyond company-specific results, Qifu Technology is contending with a difficult operating environment across China's consumer-finance sector. Management noted that short-term household consumer loan balances have contracted, reflecting voluntary and involuntary deleveraging among consumers. Regulatory oversight has also tightened across pricing, marketing, funding, collections and payments, while a late-June industry event triggered a confidence shock and sharply reduced liquidity in the loan-facilitation market. These macro and regulatory forces have compressed revenue, raised acquisition costs and constrained loan volume across the sector.

# Market Context and Trading Activity

The move came on elevated volume, with turnover running well above the stock's daily average as investors repriced the shares following the results and downgrades. The decline pushed [QFIN](https://tickeron.com/ticker/QFIN/) near its 52-week low and well below its 50-day and 200-day moving averages, reflecting sustained downward momentum that has been building since the shares traded above $32 last year. The selloff was primarily company- and sector-specific rather than a broad market event, as the stock diverged sharply from the broader U.S. indices and underscored the idiosyncratic risks facing Chinese credit-tech names.

# What Comes Next for QFIN

Looking ahead, investors will be watching for signs that loan volume and asset quality stabilize against a still-tight regulatory backdrop. Key areas of focus include the third-quarter results, trajectory of the 90-day-plus delinquency rate, funding-cost trends, and whether the company's growing fintech-technology output business — which grew sharply year over year — can offset declines in core lending revenue. Continued analyst revisions, changes in China's credit-market regulation and the pace of household deleveraging remain the principal risks and uncertainties. The company's substantial cash position and ongoing share-repurchase and dividend programs provide some balance-sheet support, but near-term sentiment is likely to remain cautious.
